questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: During which stage of mitosis do chromosomes align at the cell's equator?
questions.explanation: Chromosomes align at the metaphase plate during metaphase, which is the defining event of that stage. Prophase condenses them, anaphase pulls them apart, and telophase rebuilds nuclei, so each distractor names a real stage applied to the wrong event.
questions.hint: Which stage is defined by alignment at the equator?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Which mitotic stage is characterized by the breakdown of the nuclear envelope?
questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope fragments during prophase, allowing spindle fibers to reach chromosomes. Metaphase aligns chromosomes, anaphase separates sister chromatids, and telophase rebuilds the envelope, so each distractor names a stage with a different signature event.
questions.hint: When does the nucleus open up to the spindle?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: In which stage do sister chromatids get pulled to opposite poles of the cell?
questions.explanation: Anaphase is defined by the splitting of centromeres and movement of sister chromatids toward opposite poles via spindle fibers. Prophase condenses chromosomes, metaphase aligns them, and telophase forms new nuclei, none of which involve poleward separation.
questions.hint: Which stage literally pulls chromatids apart?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: explain the purpose of cell division
questions.stem: What is the primary purpose of mitosis in a multicellular organism?

options.misconception: confuses mitosis with meiosis crossing over

questions.explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical somatic cells that enable growth, development, and repair of damaged tissue. Gamete production, recombination, and chromosome reduction are outcomes of meiosis, not mitosis.
questions.hint: Which process keeps body cells genetically identical?

provenance.author: bank-team-b9
provenance.attestation: authored from first principles; no protected content used

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: During which phase of the cell cycle does DNA replication occur?
questions.explanation: DNA replication occurs during the S (synthesis) phase of interphase. G1 is growth, G2 is preparation for mitosis, and M phase is actual cell division, so each distractor names a real phase assigned to the wrong task.
questions.hint: Which phase is named for synthesis?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: How many daughter cells does meiosis produce from one diploid parent cell?

options.misconception: confuses meiosis I output with final output

questions.explanation: Meiosis consists of two divisions, yielding four haploid cells from one diploid parent. Mitosis yields two diploid cells, four diploid cells would require no reduction, and two haploid cells is only the product of meiosis I before the second division.
questions.hint: How many divisions occur in meiosis?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over between homologous chromosomes occur?
questions.explanation: Crossing over occurs during prophase I when homologous chromosomes pair as tetrads and exchange segments. Metaphase I aligns tetrads, anaphase I separates homologs, and prophase II has no homologous pairs left to recombine.
questions.hint: When do homologous chromosomes pair and swap segments?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: distinguish meiosis I from meiosis II
questions.stem: Which meiotic division separates homologous chromosomes rather than sister chromatids?

options.misconception: confuses second division with homolog separation

questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, reducing ploidy, while meiosis II separates sister chromatids like mitosis. Meiosis II and mitosis both split sister chromatids, and the two divisions do not both separate homologs, so the distractors misassign the separation target.
questions.hint: Which division is reductional?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: In a monohybrid cross of two heterozygous parents, what phenotypic ratio is expected in offspring?

options.misconception: confuses heterozygous cross with test cross

questions.explanation: A cross of two heterozygotes (Aa x Aa) gives genotypes 1 AA : 2 Aa : 1 aa, producing a 3 dominant to 1 recessive phenotypic ratio. A 1:1 ratio is a test cross result, inverting the ratio miscounts phenotypes, and all dominant ignores the aa class entirely.
questions.hint: Set up a Punnett square for Aa x Aa.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Two heterozygous parents (Aa x Aa) are crossed. What percentage of offspring are expected to be homozygous recessive (aa)?
questions.explanation: A Punnett square for Aa x Aa yields genotypes 25% AA, 50% Aa, and 25% aa, so one quarter of offspring are homozygous recessive.
questions.hint: Count the aa cells in a 2x2 Punnett square.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: An organism shows a dominant phenotype. Which genotype is impossible for this organism?

options.misconception: confuses a set of possible genotypes with impossible one

questions.explanation: A dominant phenotype requires at least one dominant allele, so the organism can be homozygous dominant or heterozygous but never homozygous recessive. The distractors each name genotypes that are fully compatible with a dominant phenotype, testing whether the student knows which genotype is excluded.
questions.hint: Which genotype has no dominant allele?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Why are X-linked recessive traits more commonly expressed in males than females?

options.text: Males have only one X chromosome

options.misconception: confuses male and female sex chromosomes

options.text: Females lack the recessive allele entirely
Recessive alleles are dominant in males

questions.explanation: Males are XY and carry a single X chromosome, so one recessive allele on that X is expressed with no second X to mask it. Females have two X chromosomes and need two recessive alleles to express the trait. The distractors either misstate sex chromosomes, deny carrier females, or confuse dominance rules with sex.
questions.hint: How many X chromosomes does a typical male have?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A dihybrid cross of two heterozygous parents (AaBb x AaBb) yields what classic phenotypic ratio?

options.misconception: confuses independent assortment with equal phenotypes

questions.explanation: Independent assortment in a dihybrid cross of double heterozygotes produces four phenotypic classes in a 9:3:3:1 ratio. A 3:1 ratio is monohybrid, 1:1:1:1 is a test cross result, and 9:3:4 indicates recessive epistasis rather than standard independent assortment.
questions.hint: How many phenotypic classes result from two traits?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: In a dihybrid cross (AaBb x AaBb), what percentage of offspring are expected to show both recessive phenotypes?
questions.explanation: Both recessive phenotypes require genotype aabb, which occurs with probability 1/4 for aa times 1/4 for bb, or 1/16 = 6.25%.
questions.hint: Multiply the independent probabilities for aa and bb.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: In incomplete dominance, a cross between red-flowered and white-flowered plants produces what offspring phenotype?
questions.explanation: Incomplete dominance blends the parental phenotypes, so red and white parents yield pink offspring. Red or white alone would require full dominance, and red-and-white spots describe codominance where both alleles are fully expressed rather than blended.
questions.hint: Does one allele fully mask the other?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Which human blood type system is a classic example of codominance?

options.misconception: confuses a single dominant trait with codominance
confuses disease inheritance with codominance example

questions.explanation: The ABO system is codominant: IA and IB are both fully expressed in AB individuals. Rh factor alone shows simple dominance, sickle cell is recessive inheritance, and color blindness is X-linked recessive, none of which demonstrate codominance.
questions.hint: Which system shows both A and B antigens together?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: How does cytokinesis differ between plant and animal cells?

options.text: Plant cells form a cell plate; animal cells pinch inward
Plant cells pinch inward; animal cells form a cell plate

questions.explanation: Plant cells build a cell plate from the center outward to become a new wall, while animal cells use a contractile ring that pinches the membrane into a cleavage furrow. Reversing the mechanisms, claiming both use a furrow, or denying membrane formation each misrepresents the structural difference.
questions.hint: Which cell type has a rigid wall?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Independent assortment during meiosis increases genetic variation by

options.text: Random orientation of homologous pairs at metaphase I
Exact copying of DNA during S phase
Separation of sister chromatids in meiosis II
options.misconception: confuses meiosis II with variation source

options.text: Formation of a single gamete type

questions.explanation: Independent assortment arises from the random orientation of homologous chromosome pairs at metaphase I, shuffling maternal and paternal combinations into gametes. DNA replication is high-fidelity, sister chromatid separation preserves combinations, and a single gamete type would reduce rather than increase variation.
questions.hint: When are maternal and paternal chromosomes randomly oriented?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Nondisjunction during meiosis can result in a gamete with
questions.explanation: Nondisjunction is the failure of chromosomes or chromatids to separate properly, producing gametes with extra or missing chromosomes (aneuploidy). A normal haploid set, identical chromatids only, or no DNA are not the defining outcomes of this error.
questions.hint: What happens when chromosomes fail to separate?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Down syndrome is most commonly caused by trisomy of which chromosome?

options.misconception: confuses autosomal with sex chromosome aneuploidy

questions.explanation: Down syndrome results from an extra copy of chromosome 21. Trisomy 18 causes Edwards syndrome, trisomy 13 causes Patau syndrome, and X chromosome aneuploidy causes conditions like Turner or Klinefelter syndromes rather than Down syndrome.
questions.hint: Which chromosome number names the syndrome?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Genes located close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together because of
questions.explanation: Linked genes on the same chromosome are inherited together unless separated by crossing over. Independent assortment applies to unlinked genes, crossing over does not always occur between close genes, and mutation is not an inheritance pattern for linked loci.
questions.hint: What term describes co-inheritance on one chromosome?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Spindle fibers attach to chromosomes at which specialized region?

options.misconception: confuses chromosome ends with attachment site
confuses general region with specific attachment

questions.explanation: Spindle fibers attach at the centromere, the constricted region where sister chromatids join. Telomeres cap chromosome ends, arms are not the attachment point, and nuclear pores are envelope structures unrelated to spindle attachment.
questions.hint: Where do sister chromatids join?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: The G2 checkpoint verifies that

options.text: DNA replication is complete and undamaged
The cell is large enough to divide
options.misconception: confuses G1 size check with G2

options.text: Chromosomes are aligned at the equator

questions.explanation: The G2 checkpoint confirms DNA replication is complete and checks for damage before mitosis begins. Cell size is assessed at the G1 checkpoint, chromosome alignment at the metaphase checkpoint, and cytokinesis completion occurs after division, so each distractor assigns a real check to the wrong checkpoint.
questions.hint: What must be true before entering mitosis?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Human skin color is an example of which inheritance pattern?

options.misconception: confuses maternal organelle with nuclear polygenic

questions.explanation: Skin color is controlled by multiple genes, producing continuous variation, which is polygenic inheritance. Single-gene dominant, sex-linked recessive, and mitochondrial inheritance each involve one gene or organelle rather than many additive loci.
questions.hint: How many genes influence this trait?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Epistasis occurs when

options.text: One gene masks the expression of another
Two alleles blend to form an intermediate
Both alleles are fully expressed together
A gene is expressed only in one sex

questions.explanation: Epistasis is an interaction where one gene masks or modifies the phenotypic expression of another gene. Blending describes incomplete dominance, both alleles expressed describes codominance, and sex-limited expression is a different phenomenon, so each distractor names a real genetic concept applied to the wrong interaction.
questions.hint: What does it mean for one gene to mask another?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited

options.text: Only from the father's Y chromosome

questions.explanation: Mitochondria are inherited from the egg, so mitochondrial DNA is maternal. Sperm contribute essentially no mitochondria to the zygote, nuclear DNA is biparental, and the Y chromosome is paternal sex-chromosome inheritance, so each distractor misassigns the inheritance source.
questions.hint: Which gamete contributes the mitochondria?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A heterozygous parent (Aa) is test-crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (aa). What percentage of offspring show the dominant phenotype?
questions.explanation: A test cross of Aa x aa yields 50% Aa (dominant phenotype) and 50% aa (recessive phenotype), so half the offspring show the dominant phenotype.
questions.hint: Set up a Punnett square for Aa x aa.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: A human somatic cell has 46 chromosomes. How many chromosomes are in a normal human gamete?
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, so a diploid human somatic cell with 46 chromosomes produces haploid gametes with 23 chromosomes.
questions.hint: Meiosis reduces ploidy by half.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: An organism with two identical alleles for a gene is described as

options.misconception: confuses single copy with identical pair
confuses allele state with chromosome set size

questions.explanation: Homozygous means carrying two identical alleles for a gene. Heterozygous means two different alleles, hemizygous means only one copy is present (as in X-linked genes in males), and haploid refers to a single chromosome set rather than allele identity, so each distractor names a related but distinct genetic term.
questions.hint: What term means same alleles?

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.stem: The observable physical expression of a genotype is called the

options.misconception: confuses genetic makeup with observable trait
confuses variant form with expressed trait
confuses chromosomal position with expressed trait

questions.explanation: Phenotype is the observable physical or biochemical expression of a genotype. Genotype is the underlying genetic makeup, an allele is a variant form of a gene, and a locus is a chromosomal position, so each distractor names a related genetic term rather than the expressed trait.
questions.hint: Which term describes what you can observe?
